Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the reason transphyseal distal humerus fractures are most commonly observed in
children younger than 2 years.
Discuss the difficulty in accurately diagnosing transphyseal distal humerus fractures because
of the young age of the patients who typically sustain this injury.
Explain the importance of maintaining an index of suspicion for possible nonaccidental trauma
in evaluating young children with a transphyseal distal humerus fracture.
Describe the pertinent anatomy of the supracondylar humerus and explain the reason
supracondylar humerus fractures are associated with a high rate of neurologic and/or vascular
injuries compared with other common pediatric fractures.

Distal Humerus Physeal Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
The anatomic considerations for distal humerus transphyseal fractures are the same as those
for supracondylar fractures of the distal humerus. The young age and small anatomy of the
children who typically sustain these injuries may make diagnosis and management difficult.
Epidemiology
This injury is most common in children younger than 3 years but may occur in children as old
as 6 years.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Although transphyseal fractures share the same important anatomic considerations as
supracondylar fractures, neurovascular complications are rare in patients with transphyseal
fractures.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The mechanism of injury depends on the age of the patient. In newborns and infants, a
rotatory or shear force usually is associated with birth trauma or nonaccidental trauma.
In older children, the mechanism of injury usually is a hyperextension force from a fall onto an
outstretched hand.
Injury Classification

The Salter-Harris classification system is used for these injuries; all fractures are type I or type
II.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Overview

Overview
The most challenging aspect of diagnosis is distinguishing a transphyseal fracture from
an elbow dislocation. The key to distinguishing a transphyseal separation from a true
elbow dislocation is the radial head-capitellum relationship. In an elbow dislocation, the
radial head does not articulate with the capitellum; however, in a transphyseal fracture,
the radial head-capitellum articulation remains intact. In very young patients, the
capitellum may not be ossified, which makes this distinction difficult, if not impossible. In
such patients, the correct diagnosis can be made with a high degree of suspicion and
knowledge that physeal separations are much more common than elbow dislocations in
this age group. In addition, elbow dislocations are most commonly displaced
posterolaterally; however, most transphyseal separations are displaced posteromedially.
Distinguishing transphyseal separations from lateral condyle fractures that extend
medial to the trochlear notch and produce subluxation of the ulnohumeral joint (Milch
type II fractures) also may be difficult. In both of these injuries, the radial head-
capitellum relationship remains normal. Although oblique radiographs may aid in
delineating these details, the distinction may require evaluation via arthrography or MRI
in young children with minimal ossification of the distal humeral epiphysis.
Supracondylar fractures usually occur at the level of the olecranon fossa, whereas
transphyseal separations are more distal. (Figure 1)

Patient History

Patient History
An index of suspicion for nonaccidental trauma should be maintained; therefore, careful
review of the patient history and injury is essential. Unwitnessed injuries, inconsistent or
changing explanations for the injury, and a history of multiple injuries should increase
suspicion for nonaccidental trauma and prompt immediate referral to social work
and/or child protective services. Another common history for this injury is birth trauma.
In older children, a fall onto an outstretched hand is the most common mechanism of
injury.
Physical Examination


Physical Examination
Physical examination may be even more challenging than that in children with a
supracondylar humerus fracture of the elbow. Fortunately, neurovascular injuries after
transphyseal distal humerus fractures are rare; however, assessment of pulses and
capillary refill and observation for motor function of the radial, ulnar, and median nerves
are essential. In young patients, a complete physical examination should be performed
to evaluate for bruising, burns, bite marks, and other areas of tenderness that may be
indicative of nonaccidental trauma.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Similar to supracondylar humerus fractures, obtaining good-quality radiographs of
transphyseal separations is crucial but often difficult. Occasionally, a true lateral
radiograph will reveal posterior displacement of the radius and ulna as the only sign of a
transphyseal humerus fracture. Even with high-quality radiographs, additional
evaluation may be required. Ultrasonography, MRI, and arthrography have been used in
the evaluation of transphyseal separations. Although ultrasonography is a low-cost, low-
radiation imaging modality and does not require sedation, interpretation of
ultrasonographic images is highly dependent on the experience of the operator and the
radiologist. MRI is associated with higher costs, requires sedation in young children, and
often is not readily available. Arthrography is preferred because it can be performed at
the time of definitive management. If concern for nonaccidental trauma exists, a skeletal
survey should be performed before immobilization to evaluate for other fractures.
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis

This fracture pattern often is observed in patients who have sustained nonaccidental
trauma, which should be considered in all patients. The differential diagnosis includes
supracondylar humerus fracture, lateral condyle fracture, and elbow dislocation.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning are the mainstays of management, with pin
configurations comparable to those used for supracondylar fractures. An arthrogram often is
obtained after closed reduction and pinning to confirm appropriate reduction.
Closed reduction should not be performed if the injury is diagnosed late (5 to 7 days
postinjury) to minimize the risk of iatrogenic physeal injury.

Nonsurgical Management
Because of a high rate of cubitus varus in nonsurgically treated patients, most fractures
are managed via closed reduction and pinning, with the exception of those diagnosed
late (more than 5 to 7 days postinjury).
Indications
Nonsurgical management of these injuries typically is reserved for transphyseal distal
humerus fractures that are diagnosed late.
Surgical Management
Indications
If diagnosed in a timely fashion, the preferred treatment option is closed reduction and
percutaneous pinning, often followed by intraoperative arthrography.
Techniques/Procedures
SEND FEEDBACK


Techniques/Procedures
The surgical technique is virtually identical to closed reduction and pinning of a displaced
supracondylar humerus fracture. Reduction maneuvers (gentle traction, correction of
coronal plane deformity, followed by gentle hyperflexion) and parameters for acceptable
reduction (no cubitus varus, anterior humeral line intersecting capitellum) are similar to
those for supracondylar humerus fractures. All lateral-entry pinning is preferred, with
technique and pinning pattern identical to those for supracondylar humerus fractures,
with divergent pins engaging both cortices with good spread at the fracture site. An
arthrogram commonly is obtained in combination with the procedure, either before
reduction or after reduction to confirm anatomic reduction. A posterior (preferred) or
lateral approach can be used for the arthrogram.
Complications

Complications
The most serious potential complication is failure to recognize that the injury is
secondary to nonaccidental trauma. The re-injury rate in abused children is 30% to 50%,
and the death rate in abused children is 5% to 10%.1
Orthopaedic complications are rare after prompt diagnosis and management; delayed
diagnosis frequently results in malunion that may require future osteotomy to correct
cubitus varus and/or hyperextension deformity. In addition to malunion, cubitus varus
may result from growth disturbance of the distal humerus. Neurovascular complications
are rare, which distinguishes these injuries from supracondylar humerus fractures.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Transphyseal distal humerus fractures are most commonly observed in very young children.

As many as 50% of these injuries may be caused by nonaccidental trauma, and a high index of
suspicion for potential abuse should be maintained.
Diagnosis may be difficult; arthrography is the preferred imaging modality for better
delineating the fracture pattern because definitive management can be rendered at the same
time.
Cubitus varus is a common orthopaedic complication in patients treated nonsurgically; the
mainstay of treatment is reduction and surgical stabilization.
Pediatric Polytrauma and Upper Extremity Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Supracondylar humerus fractures account for approximately 50% of all pediatric elbow
fractures and are most frequently observed in children aged 3 to 10 years.
The high incidence of residual deformity and the potential for neurovascular complications
make supracondylar humerus fractures a serious injury.
Epidemiology
Supracondylar humerus fractures account for more than one-half of pediatric elbow fractures.
Extension-type injuries account for 95% to 98% of supracondylar humerus fractures.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Distal humerus anatomy is shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2 Illustration of an elbow shows the anatomy of the distal humerus.
Osteology
The elbow joint consists of three articulating bones that allow for motion in three planes.
The distal humerus has unique relationships with the radius and ulna that make three-
dimensional mobility possible. The radiocapitellar articulation allows for pronation and
supination of the forearm, and the ulnohumeral articulation allows for flexion and extension
of the elbow.
The medial and lateral columns comprising the distal humerus are separated by a thin area of
bone that contains a fossa for the coronoid of the ulna anteriorly and a fossa for the olecranon
posteriorly. This thin area of bone ultimately represents a zone of vulnerability through which
most supracondylar humerus fractures originate.1
Vascular Anatomy
The brachial artery lies anterior to the distal humerus, traversing the antecubital fossa.
The artery may be tented over the distal humerus after a displaced extension-type
supracondylar humerus fracture. It also may become entrapped between fracture fragments
during attempted reduction of the fracture.
Neural Anatomy
The median nerve traverses the antecubital fossa, just medial to the brachial artery.

Laterally, the radial nerve crosses from posterior to anterior at a distance from the distal
humeral physis calculated by the patient’s age multiplied by 1 cm in children younger than 6
years. In children 6 years or older, the radial nerve crosses over laterally at a distance more
than 6 cm from the distal humeral physis.2
The ulnar nerve passes posteriorly behind the medial epicondyle.
Musculature
The brachialis muscle is anterior to the distal humerus and can be pierced by the proximal
fracture fragment.
This buttonholing of the proximal fragment occurs may cause a puckering of the skin along the
antecubital fossa, often termed the brachialis sign.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The thin area of bone between the medial and lateral columns is a vulnerable zone through
which most supracondylar humerus fractures of the elbow originate.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
If the elbow is forced into hyperextension, the olecranon can act as a fulcrum through
which an extension force can propagate a fracture across the medial and lateral
columns. Similarly, a force applied posteriorly with the elbow in flexion may create a
fracture originating at the level of the olecranon fossa. Therefore, whether the result of
an extension or flexion force, supracondylar humerus fractures typically are transverse
and at the level of the olecranon fossa.
Associated Injuries
Vascular injuries occur in approximately 1% of patients with a supracondylar humerus
fracture.
Nerve injuries occur in 10% to 15% of patients with a supracondylar humerus fracture.
Additional bony injuries may occur at the time that a supracondylar humerus fracture is
sustained.


Associated Injuries
Because of the rich collateral flow at the elbow, distal perfusion may remain adequate
despite a brachial artery injury.
With posterolaterally displaced fractures, the median nerve and the anterior
interosseous nerve (AIN) are most commonly at risk for injury/neuropraxia from the
metaphyseal spike of the proximal fragment tenting anteromedially. The ulnar nerve is
at greatest risk in patients with a flexion-type injury. In patients with a posteromedial
fracture, the radial nerve is at greatest risk.
The most common concomitant bony injury is a distal radius fracture, which is
associated with an incidence of 5% after supracondylar humerus fracture.1 This suggests
a higher level of injury to the upper extremity; therefore, great attention should be paid
to the neurovascular status of the child. Although previous studies have implicated a
high risk of compartment syndrome in patients with a floating elbows,3,4 a more recent
systemic review reported a 2% rate of pediatric acute compartment syndrome with
these injuries.5
Injury Classification
The modified Gartland classification system is used to classify supracondylar humerus
fractures.
Type I fractures are nondisplaced (Figure 3).
Type II fractures (Figure 4) have angulation of the distal fragment, with one cortex remaining
intact (the posterior cortex remains intact in extension-type injuries and the anterior remains
in flexion-type injuries).
Type III (Figure 5) injuries are completely displaced, with both cortices fractured.


Injury Classification
A modified Gartland type IV injury (Resource 1), in which the fracture is unstable in
flexion and extension because of circumferential disruption of the periosteum, also
exists. This typically is only apparent during surgical manipulation and management;
however, radiographic injury parameters of flexion angulation, valgus angulation, lateral

translation, and cortical apposition of the distal and proximal fragments are associated
with a greater risk of the fracture being a type IV injury rather than a type III injury.6
Surgeons must note the displacement of the distal fracture fragment in the coronal
plane. The common scenario is for the distal fragment to be displaced medially. More
concerning is the posterolaterally displaced type III fracture. Although this injury pattern
occurs less frequently, accounting for 25% of extension supracondylar fractures, it is
more commonly associated with neurovascular injuries. This is because the proximal
fragment is displaced anteromedially in the direction of the neurovascular bundle.
Assessment of the coronal plane also is important because medial column collapse
leading to varus orientation of the distal humerus is an indication for reduction and
surgical stabilization, even in patients who appear to have a nondisplaced fracture in the
sagittal plane.
Most supracondylar fractures are closed injuries. Open fractures are classified according
to the Gustilo-Anderson classification system.
Mechanics of Fractures
Supracondylar humerus fractures may result from an extension or flexion force on the distal
humerus.
Extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures account for approximately 95% of all
supracondylar fractures.
With hyperextension injuries the distal fragment will be displaced posteriorly.
Flexion-type supracondylar fractures are rare and occur in only approximately 5% of patients.
The mechanism of flexion in supracondylar fractures usually is a direct blow on the posterior
aspect of a flexed elbow, which results in anterior displacement of the distal fragment.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

The typical patient history consists of a fall onto an outstretched hand, which causes
hyperextension of the elbow.
Occasionally, the mechanism of injury is a direct blow on the posterior aspect of a flexed
elbow.
Physical Examination
A complete and thorough assessment of the neurologic function of the hand is essential in
treating a child with a supracondylar humerus fracture.

Physical Examination
A comprehensive sensory and motor examination often is difficult in very young children
with an acute elbow fracture. If a gentle effort is made, most children aged 3 or 4 years
will cooperate with a sensory and directed motor examination. For distressed children
who cannot cooperate with a directed examination, a sensory examination can be
performed by submerging the hand of the injured extremity in warm water for several
minutes.7 Lack of skin wrinkling in the sensory distribution of a peripheral nerve (most
commonly the median nerve in a supracondylar humerus fracture) or lack of sweat
pattern from interruption of neural input to the sudomotor sweat glands indicates nerve
injury.
If a complete examination is not possible, surgeons must forewarn the parents of the
10% to 15% likelihood that a neurologic injury will be discovered at the time a thorough
examination can be performed.1 Fortunately, patients with these injuries almost always
do well, with median time to nerve recovery being 2.3 months.8
Neurovascular Examination
The motor and sensory function of the median, radial, and ulnar nerves must be assessed.
Vascular examination, including assessment of the radial pulse and clinical inspection for signs
of forearm and hand ischemia, is essential.


Neurovascular Examination
Asking about diminished or abnormal sensation and testing for light touch are the basics
of neurovascular evaluation. Testing for two-point discrimination may be more sensitive
in the identification of a sensory deficit; however, it is not routinely performed because
most patients are cognitively unable to comply with this test until they are grade-school
age. Testing areas via single sensory nerve innervation helps identify specific deficits in
the median (palmar distal index finger), radial (dorsal first web space), and ulnar (palmar
distal little finger) nerves. The AIN is the most commonly injured nerve and is solely a
motor nerve; therefore, no sensory deficits are observed with AIN neuropraxia. AIN palsy
results in weakness of flexion and resting extension of the distal interphalangeal joint of
the index finger and interphalangeal joint of the thumb. Weak or absent
metacarpophalangeal joint extension is a sign of radial nerve palsy, whereas inability to
spread the fingers widely or flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the little finger while
holding the proximal interphalangeal joint extended identifies ulnar nerve motor deficit.
A patient with a supracondylar fracture and a complete median nerve palsy must be
monitored more closely preoperatively and postoperatively for the development of
compartment syndrome. This scenario is problematic because one of the earliest signs
of developing compartment syndrome after a supracondylar fracture is dysesthesia in
the median nerve distribution in the hand and progressive weakness of finger flexion,
both of which cannot be assessed in patients with median nerve palsy.8
Although a complete neurologic examination may not always be possible, depending on
the age of the child, it is always possible to assess the vascular status of patients with a
displaced supracondylar humerus fracture. If the radial pulse is nonpalpable, Doppler
may be used to assess flow. Other physical examination signs, such as color, perfusion,
and warmth of the limb, should be evaluated.
Surgeons must be diligent in monitoring for clinical signs of developing compartment
syndrome. The earliest sign of compartment syndrome is pain out of proportion with
physical examination findings. In pediatric patients, the three As of anxiety, agitation,
and increased analgesic pain medication requirements are better indicators of an
impending compartment syndrome than the five Ps of pallor, pulselessness, pain,

paresthesias, and paralysis.9 If these signs are recognized in patients with a
supracondylar humerus fracture, urgent forearm fasciotomies and stabilization of the
supracondylar humerus are indicated.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The only radiographic finding in patients with a nondisplaced supracondylar humerus fracture
often is a positive anterior or posterior fat pad sign.
With displaced fractures, a common radiographic parameter that is assessed on AP
radiographs is the Baumann angle.
In addition to assessing for the fat pads of the elbow, several additional radiographic
parameters can be assessed on lateral radiographs.
Hourglass
Anterior humeral line
Humerocapitellar angle
Coronoid line

Radiography
The anterior fat pad is a triangular radiolucency anterior to the distal humeral diaphysis;
it is observed clearly and, in patients with elbow effusion, it is displaced anteriorly. The
posterior fat pad is not normally visible if the elbow is flexed at right angles; however, if
an effusion is present, it is visible posteriorly.
The Baumann angle is the angle between the physeal line of the lateral condyle of the
humerus and a line drawn perpendicular to the long axis of the humeral shaft. Some
variability exists in the normal value of this angle (8° to 28°); however, a side-to-side
difference of more than 5° may indicate a coronal plane deformity that warrants surgical
reduction and stabilization.

The distal humerus should project as a teardrop or hourglass, the distal aspect of which
is formed by the ossific center of the capitellum. It should appear as an almost perfect
circle. An imperfect circle or an obscured hourglass implies an oblique orientation of the
distal portion of the humerus from an inadequate radiographic technique or fracture
displacement. In addition, the angle formed by the long axis of the humerus and the
long axis of the capitellum should be approximately 40°. In supracondylar fractures with
posterior tilting of the distal fragment (observed with extension fractures), the
humerocapitellar angle will diminish, whereas with anterior tilting of the distal fragment,
the humerocapitellar angle will increase. The anterior humeral line—a line drawn
through the anterior cortex of the distal humerus—should pass through the middle third
of the ossific nucleus of the capitellum. In children younger than 4 years, the line may
pass more anteriorly through the capitellum than in older children. With extension
supracondylar fractures, the anterior humeral line will pass anterior to the middle of the
capitellum, whereas with flexion injuries, it will pass posteriorly. Finally, the coronoid
line, a line projected superiorly along the anterior border of the coronoid process,
should just touch the anterior border of the lateral condyle of the humerus; however,
with displaced extension supracondylar fractures, the coronoid line will pass anterior to
the anterior border of the lateral condyle.1
Computed Tomography
CT is rarely, if ever, necessary in the diagnosis and management of pediatric supracondylar
humerus fractures.
The lone exception is in adolescents with a distal humerus fracture who may have intra-
articular extension.
Differential Diagnosis
Transphyseal distal humerus fracture
Elbow dislocation
Lateral condyle fracture

Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis for severely displaced supracondylar humerus fractures
includes transphyseal distal humerus fractures, elbow dislocations, and unstable Milch
type II lateral condyle fractures. True elbow dislocations are relatively uncommon and
generally are observed in older children. They most commonly are associated with
medial epicondyle fractures. Transphyseal distal humerus fractures are more common
than supracondylar fractures in children younger than 2 years but are uncommon in
children older than 2 years. Transphyseal fractures are associated with child abuse in as
many as 50% of patients.10 Unstable lateral condyle fractures can be differentiated from
supracondylar fractures most readily on the lateral radiograph. Supracondylar fractures
usually originate at the olecranon fossa and typically are transverse. Lateral condyle
fractures originate more distally, often with only a small metaphyseal fragment visible on
lateral radiographs; an oblique radiograph also is useful for better defining a lateral
condyle fracture. On AP radiographs, an unstable lateral condyle fracture (Milch type II)
may have a normal-appearing radiocapitellar joint but will demonstrate subluxation of
the ulnotrochlear joint. Conversely, a Milch type I lateral condyle fracture will have a

following criteria are met:

The anterior humeral line intersects the capitellum after reduction
No medial cortical impaction of the distal humerus and/or varus malalignment is present.

immobilization of an injured elbow in hyperflexion may lead to additional swelling,
increased compartment pressure, and possibly the development of Volkmann ischemic

swelling subsides postinjury, a cast may loosen and allow the elbow to extend, which
may result in loss of reduction. This may occur even after the first follow-up radiograph
demonstrates maintenance of the reduction. Varus hyperextension malunion is not
discovered until the cast is removed a few weeks later. Therefore, patients with a type IIa
supracondylar humerus fracture managed via reduction and cast immobilization should
be seen in the outpatient setting at least twice within the first 14 days after the initial
injury. Although good results can be attained with cast immobilization in patients with a
type II fracture, the necessity to immobilize the elbow in flexion and the unpredictable
complication of loss of reduction have led to a decline in the use of cast immobilization
for supracondylar fractures that require reduction.1 The American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons clinical practice guidelines generally favor reduction and pinning
of type II supracondylar humerus fractures.12

Indications
Most type II and all type III and IV fractures are managed via reduction and pinning under
general anesthesia in the operating room.

Closed Reduction Technique
Traction is applied with the elbow in full extension to reduce the coronal plane deformity.
In a typical extension-type fracture, the elbow is flexed to reduce the sagittal plane.
Forearm pronation may assist in reduction of medially displaced fractures, and supination may
assist in reduction of laterally displaced fractures.

Closed Reduction Technique
Under general anesthesia, the child is placed in the supine position on the surgical table.
If ipsilateral forearm radiographs have not been obtained to rule out forearm injury, this
is an opportunity to obtain such imaging studies. If a brachialis sign is observed, the
milking maneuver can be performed to extricate the entrapped metaphyseal spike from
the brachialis muscle fibers. To reduce the elbow fracture, traction is applied with the
elbow in full extension. An assistant grasps the proximal humerus firmly to allow the
surgeon to pull traction on the distal fragment. After adequate traction has been
applied, the coronal plane deformity is corrected as traction is maintained. Continuing to
maintain traction with one hand, the surgeon uses the fingers of the opposite hand to
apply a posterior force to the proximal fragment. The thumb of this hand is then
advanced along the posterior humeral shaft to milk the distal fragment further distally.
After the thumb reaches the olecranon, it applies an anterior force to the distal fragment
as the fingers continue to push the proximal fragment posteriorly. The hand holding
traction then flexes the elbow and pronates or supinates the forearm, depending on
displacement of the distal fragment (pronation for posteromedially displaced fractures
and supination for posterolateral fractures). As the elbow is being flexed, the surgeon
can continue to exert a distracting force on the distal fragment. With the elbow
hyperflexed, reduction is assessed on AP and lateral views. The lateral image can be
obtained by externally rotating the shoulder or rotating the image intensifier; however,
with very unstable fractures, the surgeon may need to rotate the image intensifier to
avoid displacing the fracture. After reduction has been confirmed, the fracture can be
immobilized via percutaneous pin fixation.1 (Video 1)

Fracture Fixation and Pin Configuration
Two or three 0.062-inch smooth Kirschner wires (K-wires) typically are used for
surgical stabilization of these fractures.
Lateral-entry pins are the current standard of care for most injuries, with a medial pin
added for unstable variants.

Fracture Fixation and Pin Configuration
In laboratory studies, crossed pins are more stable biomechanically than lateral-
entry pins.15,16 Using a medial pin traditionally was thought to result in a
substantially increased risk of iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury, especially if the
medial pin is inserted with the elbow fully flexed. Therefore, most surgeons
currently use two or three lateral-entry pins for fracture fixation. A medial pin is
added only if adequate fracture stability cannot be achieved with the use of
three lateral-entry pins. If using a medial pin, a small incision can be made
directly over the medial epicondyle, with blunt dissection performed via a
hemostat onto bone to ensure that the ulnar nerve is not injured by the pin.
Extending the elbow during placement of this pin also minimizes potential injury
to the nerve.
Lateral-entry pins should be separated sufficiently to engage the medial and
lateral columns of the distal humerus at the level of the fracture. The pin spread
should be at least 14 mm, or one-third the width of the humerus at the level of
the fracture, to minimize potential loss of reduction.17 If inserted with
appropriate technique, lateral-entry pins are comparable to a crossed-pin
configuration with regard to maintaining reduction of supracondylar humerus
fractures. Three pins are biomechanically stronger than two pins in bending and
torsion. In addition, iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury does not occur with lateral-
entry pins.

Preoperative Planning and Patient Positioning
Surgeons must have a consistent operating room setup in the management of
these fractures. Many surgeons prefer to use an inverted fluoroscopy machine
as a surgical table; however, because of potential instability and the difficulty in
maintaining reduction in some displaced type III supracondylar humerus
fractures, the procedure should be performed on a radiolucent table. The
fracture may be too unstable to rotate the arm to obtain a lateral view. In these
patients, a lateral fluoroscopic view of the fracture, obtained by rotating the arc
of the fluoroscopy machine to 90°, often is necessary. The surgical table is
rotated to 90° to align the fluoroscopic arm parallel with the bed. The
fluoroscopy machine is positioned at the head of the bed so that the C-arm is
easily rotated for a lateral fluoroscopic view without the image intensifier hitting
the bed.18

mass
Lateral: used for posteromedial injuries

controversial.

reduction and stabilization generally can be closely observed without the immediate
need for open exploration.

Management of Pink, Pulseless Supracondylar Humerus
Fractures
The optimal management of a pulseless but perfused hand after supracondylar
humerus fracture remains controversial. The abundant collateral circulation of
the elbow allows the distal extremity to remain viable despite complete
disruption of the brachial artery. Some surgeons advocate for aggressive
surgical attempts to restore a normal pulse because of concerns that
nonsurgical management of a pulseless viable extremity may lead to
progressive ischemia from thrombus formation or subsequent problems with
cold intolerance, exercise claudication, or growth discrepancy.
A single-center study reviewed more than 1,200 patients with a supracondylar
humerus fracture, 54 of whom presented with no palpable radial pulse.20 Five
of the patients (9%) underwent vascular repair to restore blood flow. All the
patients who underwent exploration had no Doppler pulses after closed
reduction and percutaneous pinning, and all the patients had an arterial injury
that was repaired. In this series, the absence of a palpable pulse after closed
reduction and percutaneous pinning was not an absolute indication to proceed
with vascular exploration if clinical findings suggested that the distal aspect of
the forearm and hand were well perfused (ie, a Doppler signal and a brisk
capillary refill); however, these patients should be admitted and closely
observed postoperatively via serial examinations. An absent radial pulse by
palpation in a patient with a type-III supracondylar humerus fracture may
indicate substantial vascular and neurologic injury; however, in the experience
of many surgeons, patients with no palpable radial pulse who have a perfused
limb (ie, warm, pink, and with brisk capillary refill) and a pulse detected via
Doppler ultrasonography after closed reduction and percutaneous pinning can
be closely observed postoperatively rather than treated via immediate open
vascular exploration, whereas patients with no radial pulse detected via Doppler
ultrasonography after closed reduction and percutaneous pinning should
increase suspicion for arterial injury.20 (Video 2)

Volkmann contracture results from compression of the brachial artery and/or
severe soft-tissue swelling in the forearm from cast immobilization in
substantial elbow flexion. It also may result from a missed compartment
syndrome associated with a supracondylar humerus fracture.

Malunion
Cubitus varus after supracondylar humerus fracture occurs because of a
malunion rather than a growth disturbance.
Little potential exists for angular malunion of the distal humerus to remodel.
Cubitus varus is a three-dimensional deformity of varus, extension, and
internal rotation.
If deformity is severe or interfering with function, surgical reconstruction is
indicated.
Most corrective osteotomies focus on correction of varus and extension.

Malunion
Cubitus varus (gunstock deformity) is a cosmetic deformity with few
functional sequelae in childhood; however, it may increase the risk for
subsequent lateral condyle fracture. The incidence is much lower with
reduction and pinning than with closed reduction and cast
immobilization. It results from malreduction or loss of reduction rather
than growth disturbance after fracture.
Cubitus varus or valgus is assessed by measuring the carrying angle of
the arm. This is the angle created by the medial border of the fully
supinated forearm and the medial border of the humerus with the
elbow extended. As the elbow extends, the carrying angle decreases
(more varus); therefore, hyperextension tends to accentuate a cubitus
varus deformity, whereas a flexion contracture may create the
appearance of cubitus valgus.

the distal humerus to remodel. Therefore, the best treatment option
for malunion of a supracondylar humerus fracture is prevention.
Awareness of the pitfalls associated with attaining and maintaining
adequate reduction will help minimize the occurrence of malunion and
the degree of deformity if it does occur. Because cubitus valgus and
varus primarily are cosmetic deformities, mild degrees of malunion can
be managed via simple reassurance; however, if the deformity is
severe, cosmetic concerns or, less commonly, functional limitations
may warrant surgical reconstruction. Evidence in the adult literature
shows that long-standing cubitus varus deformity may lead to
complications, such as posterolateral rotatory instability, tardy ulnar
nerve palsy, and radial head dislocation that may not resolve even after
distal humeral osteotomy and lateral ulnar collateral ligament
reconstruction.22
The resultant cubitus varus deformity is a three-dimensional deformity
of varus, extension, and internal rotation. Most corrective osteotomies
focus on the correction of varus and extension deformity. The
rotational deformity is well tolerated and best left unmanaged because
rotation of the distal fragment makes the osteotomy unstable. Some
studies have cited few complications;23 however, earlier studies noted
complication rates between 30% and 50%.24-26 Parents should
understand that surgical reconstruction is a technically demanding
procedure intended primarily to improve cosmesis and regain elbow
flexion, if limited. The approach most used for corrective osteotomy is a
laterally based closing wedge osteotomy, along with correction of the
extension deformity. This is performed via a lateral approach to the
distal humerus and can be fixed with the use of all lateral-entry pins or
via a cross-pin technique.1
